stories.title: Japan PM calls official residence ‘workplace’, sees cockroach but not ghosts
stories.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Aug 22 that she uses her official residence near her office as a workplace, in an apparent response to views that she tends to seclude herself in her house. In a series of posts on social media platform X, Takaichi also said she has not seen ghosts inside the residence, which is often rumoured to be haunted, but that she has encountered a cockroach despite doing the household work herself. Takaichi, who became prime minister in October, moved into the residence located next to the prime minister’s office in late December. “I’ve created an environment to work both at the office and the official residence. This has allowed me to make necessary judgements and take responses swiftly, be it early in the morning or at night or on holidays,” Takaichi said. She has tried to use her official residence more often to “reduce the burden on staff at the prime minister’s office”, because doing so requires fewer security and other personnel. While media outlets report that she spent “the whole day at the official residence”, she said: “I perform the necessary duties.” Takaichi has seen her public support slip in recent opinion polls, while she pushed for key agendas, including a revision of the Imperial House Law that maintains a male-only succession system and a temporary reduction in the consumption tax on food items. Despite topping the 2025 buzzword list, her pledge to “work, work, work, work and work” – made after being elected head of the ruling party – caused a stir. It prompted criticism from those calling for workstyle reforms and a better “work-life” balance. In July, she also said on X: “Zero to three hours of sleep has become the norm” since becoming premier, adding that she spends her nights reviewing documents until dawn while doing household chores. The official residence is where then Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai was assassinated in a coup attempt in 1932 and the primary site of another failed coup four years later.

stories.title: US returns dozens of smuggled artifacts from three different eras to Egypt
stories.summary: American spy agency FBI returned dozens of looted artifacts to Egyptian government officials during a ceremony held Friday in Los Angeles. Among the items returned to were jewelry, statues, sculptures, along with other pieces dating back to the Pharaonic, Roman, and Coptic periods, according to the FBI. The items were recovered from a smuggler who has since passed away. "This is an ongoing investigation, so we're not going to go into a lot of the details primarily. Despite knowing that the suspected trafficker is now deceased, we are seeking to identify further co-conspirators. And additionally, we have reason to believe there may be more items out there," according to Allen Grove, Special Agent on the FBI Art Crime Team 18. According to the FBI, US law enforcement agencies have returned more than 5,000 archaeological and cultural artifacts to Egypt over the past decade. "These artifacts are an integral part of our people's identity, of their cultural heritage, their history, and it's truly a great honor to see that our partnership with the US allows us to bring them home and to bring them where they belong," said Hossam Eldeen Aly, the Egyptian Consul General in Los Angeles. In 2016, the US and Egypt signed an agreement on cultural property, allowing the US to impose restrictions on the import of certain categories of archaeological and ethnological materials from Egypt.

stories.title: Antwerp's 'human zoo': Belgium confronts shame of colonial past
stories.summary: In 1894, when the Belgian city of Antwerp was hosting a World's Fair, more than a hundred Congolese people were forcibly brought to the city to be exhibited in the Congo Pavilion. In this "human zoo", seven Congolese men ultimately died of disease. Today, this shocking episode still haunts Belgium as one of its colonial history's darkest chapters. This year, a monument to the victims was unveiled. Report by Alix le Bourbon and Dave Keating.
